A (Introduction to Fields)

A2

Words: 316 Articles: 6
A OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 126 Articles: 1
A2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 126
a OurBigBook.com
A splitting field of f over F is a field extension K/F in which f is a product of linear factors and which is generated over F by its roots. The generation condition rules out adjoining unrelated elements.
For existence, induct on the degree of a polynomial. Choose an irreducible polynomial divisor p of f. The quotient ring F[X]/(p) is a field because (p) is a maximal ideal; the class α of X is a root of p, hence of f. Over this field extension, divide out X−α and apply induction to the remaining polynomial. This gives an extension in which f splits. Inside it, the subfield generated by all roots is a splitting field. The induction starts with a linear polynomial, whose splitting field is already F. Thus every positive-degree polynomial has a splitting field; being monic is unnecessary for existence.

The cubic has no root in F2​, since its values at 0 and 1 are both 1. A cubic over a field is irreducible precisely when it has no root. Consequently
K=F2​[α],α3+α+1=0,
(1)
is a field extension of degree 3, with eight elements. The Frobenius endomorphism x↦x2 takes a root of a polynomial over F2​ to another root, so the roots are α,α2,α4. They are distinct: equality between any two would make the Frobenius endomorphism orbit have length less than 3, contradicting the minimal polynomial of α. They all lie in K, and one of them generates K. Hence
K≅F8​,[K:F2​]=3.​
(2)

Solution
Words: 87
c OurBigBook.com
The roots are ±2​ and ±3​, so the splitting field is K=Q(2​,3​). The first adjunction has degree 2. To see that the second does too, suppose 3​=u+v2​ with u,v∈Q. Squaring and comparing rational and irrational parts gives uv=0 and u2+2v2=3. If v=0, then u2=3; if u=0, then v2=3/2. Neither is a rational square, as follows by comparing prime exponents in numerator and denominator. Thus 3​∈/Q(2​). The tower law now yields
[K:Q]=4,K=Q(2​,3​).​
(3)
A basis is 1,2​,3​,6​.

a OurBigBook.com
A composition series is a finite chain
1=G0​◃G1​◃⋯◃Gr​=G
(4)
whose inclusions are strict and whose quotients Gi​/Gi−1​ are simple. These quotients are the composition factors. The normal subgroup condition is relative to the next member, rather than necessarily to all of G.
Induct on the order of a finite group. The trivial group has the empty composition series. Otherwise choose a maximal normal subgroup N⪇G, which exists because there are finitely many subgroups. The subgroup correspondence theorem identifies normal subgroups of G/N with normal subgroups of G containing N, so maximality makes G/N a simple group. By induction N has a composition series; appending G gives one for G.
For example, the nonabelian symmetric group S3​ has
1◃A3​◃S3​,
(5)
with composition factors C3​ and C2​, both abelian.

b

Words: 57 Articles: 1
B2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 57
b OurBigBook.com
In the Klein four-group V={1,a,b,ab}, the chains
1◃⟨a⟩◃V,1◃⟨b⟩◃V
(6)
are distinct composition series. All their composition factors are C2​.
The Jordan–Hölder theorem states that any two composition series of a group have the same length and the same composition factors up to permutation and group isomorphism. Thus the subgroup chains may differ, while the multiset of simple quotients is intrinsic.

Write Cn​=⟨g⟩ and set N=⟨gp⟩. The order of gp is n/gcd(n,p)=m, so N≅Cm​. Every subgroup of an abelian group is a normal subgroup. The quotient group Cn​/N is generated by gN and has order n/m=p, hence is Cp​ and is a simple group. By the subgroup correspondence theorem, there is no proper normal subgroup strictly between N and Cn​. Therefore N is a maximal normal subgroup with the required quotient group.

d OurBigBook.com
Suppose
n=p1​⋯pr​=q1​⋯qs​
(7)
are two factorizations into primes. Repeatedly apply the cyclic-subgroup construction of part (c), first removing pr​, then pr−1​, and so on. This constructs a composition series for Cn​ whose composition factors are Cp1​​,…,Cpr​​. The second factorization constructs another composition series with composition factors Cq1​​,…,Cqs​​.
By the Jordan–Hölder theorem, r=s and these composition factors agree up to group isomorphism and permutation. Since isomorphic finite groups have the same order, the corresponding primes agree. This proves uniqueness of prime factorization up to permutation, using existence of prime factorizations but not their uniqueness.

Words: 161 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 161
iii OurBigBook.com
Every integer square remains a square modulo every prime number, including the zero class at its prime divisors. Conversely, let a be an odd integer which is not an integer square. If a is the negative of a square, part (i) supplies an odd k with (a/k)=−1. In every other case, the prime factorization of ∣a∣ has an odd exponent t at some odd prime q. Write a=±qtb with b>0 odd and gcd(q,b)=1, and apply part (ii).
In either case, factor the resulting k into primes. Since its Jacobi symbol is a product of Legendre symbols and equals −1, at least one prime factor p has (a/p)=−1. Thus a is not a square modulo that prime. This proves an odd integer is an integer square exactly when it is a square modulo every prime. If the phrase quadratic residue is restricted to nonzero residue classes, the final statement must instead say “a square modulo every prime”; for example, 9 reduces to zero modulo 3.

E3

Words: 386 Articles: 1
E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 386
E3 OurBigBook.com
A connected space has no expression as the union of two disjoint nonempty open subsets. A continuous surjection to the two-point discrete space would pull back its singleton sets to such a separation. Conversely, a separation X=U⊔V defines a continuous surjection by taking the values 0 on U and 1 on V. Thus these two conditions are equivalent, including for the empty space.
If a subset S⊆R contains a<c but omits some b between them, its intersections with (−∞,b) and (b,∞) separate it. Hence every nonempty connected subset is an interval. Conversely, let an interval I have a separation and choose a<b in its opposite sides. Restrict the associated two-valued continuous function to [a,b]⊆I and regard it as a real-valued function. The intermediate value theorem forces the value 1/2, a contradiction. Singletons and the empty set are connected directly.
For the union assertion, let u:X→{0,1} be continuous. Each restriction u∣Ai​​ is constant because Ai​ is connected. Since every pair of the Ai​ intersects, these constants agree, so u is constant on X. There is no continuous surjection, and X is connected. The empty indexing case gives X=∅ and is harmless.
To apply this to the plane, for each t∈R take the union of the horizontal line at height t with the vertical axis. Its two lines are connected and intersect; all such unions share the vertical axis and cover R2. Thus the plane is connected. For the punctured plane, take, for every r>0, the circle of radius r together with the positive horizontal ray. The circle is the continuous image of [0,2π], and intersects that connected ray. These unions share the ray and cover R2∖{0}, so the punctured plane is connected too. Translation gives the same conclusion after removing any one point.
Finally, suppose g:R2→R were a continuous injection. Its image I is a connected interval with at least three points. Choose an interior point c of I and its unique preimage p. The restriction of g to R2∖{p} is a continuous surjection onto I∖{c}. Its domain is connected, whereas its image is separated by the two half-lines on either side of c. This contradicts preservation of connectedness under continuous images. Therefore no continuous injection of the plane into the line exists.

Solution

E4 OurBigBook.com
A metric space is sequentially compact if every sequence has a convergent subsequence whose limit belongs to the space. A limit point ℓ of S is a point for which every open ball about ℓ contains a point of S other than ℓ.
Let (xn​) lie in a compact metric space. If one value occurs infinitely often, take a constant subsequence. Otherwise its set of values S is infinite. If S had no limit point, every point of the space would have a neighborhood containing at most one member of S. A finite subcover of these neighborhoods would force S finite, a contradiction. Thus S has a limit point; the stated subsequence result supplies a convergent subsequence. This proves sequential compactness.
Assume now that X is nonempty, as is necessary for the requested minimum and fixed point. The function r(x)=d(f(x),x) is continuous, as a composition of x↦(f(x),x) with the metric. The extreme value theorem on a compact space implies that r attains its infimum, say at p. If f(p)=p, strict decrease of distances gives
r(f(p))=d(f2(p),f(p))<d(f(p),p)=r(p),
(42)
contradicting minimality. Thus f(p)=p. If p,q were distinct fixed points, then d(p,q)=d(f(p),f(q))<d(p,q), another contradiction. Hence there is exactly one fixed point. This is the fixed point theorem for a strictly distance-decreasing map on a compact metric space.
Compactness is essential. On R, take
f(x)=log(1+ex).​
(43)
Here f(x)−x=log(1+e−x)>0, so there is no fixed point. Nevertheless 0<f′(x)=ex/(1+ex)<1 everywhere, and the mean value theorem gives ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<∣x−y∣ for distinct x,y. There is no uniform Lipschitz constant less than 1, since f′(x)→1 as x→∞.

For a regular isoperimetric constraint, introduce a constant Lagrange multiplier λ and set L=F−λG. With fixed endpoint values, the Euler-Lagrange equation is
Ly​−dxd​Ly′​=0.​
(56)
If F and G have no explicit x dependence, the Beltrami identity gives the first integral
L−y′Ly′​=constant.
(57)
The regularity assumption excludes the exceptional case in which the constraint itself has zero first variation for every admissible perturbation.
Parametrize the surface of revolution by r(z,θ)=(f(z)cosθ,f(z)sinθ,z). The magnitude of rz​×rθ​ is f1+f′2​. Integrating the resulting surface area element over θ, and integrating the circular cross-sectional areas for the volume, gives
A=2π∫ab​f1+f′2​dz,V=π∫ab​f2dz.
(58)
Here f≥0 because it is a radius. For a regular connected closed surface, take f>0 in the interior; the closing endpoints can have unbounded f′ even when the surface itself is smooth.
After dividing A−λV by π, its integrand is L=2f1+f′2​−λf2. The Euler-Lagrange equation and Beltrami identity become
1+f′2​−λf−dzd​(1+f′2​ff′​)=0,1+f′2​2f​−λf2=C.
(59)
As f tends to zero at an endpoint, 0≤2f/1+f′2​≤2f also tends to zero, so C=0. On the positive interior this implies λ>0 and, writing R=2/λ,
1+f′2=f2R2​.
(60)
The Euler-Lagrange equation also yields f′′=−R2/f3. Therefore
(f2)′′=2(f′2+ff′′)=−2,
(61)
including at the maximum where f′=0. Integrating and using the first integral gives
f(z)2=R2−(z−z0​)2.
(62)
Thus the regular extremal is a sphere. The two zeros fix its center and radius:
z0​=2a+b​,R=2b−a​,λ=R2​=b−a4​.​
(63)
Equivalently, the prescribed volume fixes R=(3V/(4π))1/3. If a,b are fixed in advance, their separation and the prescribed volume must be compatible with these equations; there is no positive regular stationary profile of the stated type for an incompatible volume.
For minimality, the three-dimensional isoperimetric inequality states that every sufficiently regular closed surface enclosing volume V has
A3≥36πV2,
(64)
with equality precisely for a sphere. Our extremal has A=4πR2 and V=4πR3/3, so it attains equality and is a global minimum of area at the fixed volume. This also makes clear the connected-surface assumption behind uniqueness: allowing several disconnected components introduces stationary collections of spheres, rather than the single positive generating profile used here.

On ζ=aeiθ, the Joukowski map gives z=2acosθ, so the image is the segment S=[−2a,2a]. Solving the resulting quadratic gives the inverse candidates
ζ=21​(z±z2−4a2​).
(72)
On D=C∖[−2a,2a], choose the analytic square root s(z) of z2−4a2 characterized by s(z)/z→1 at infinity. One explicit definition is
s(z)=(z+2a)z+2az−2a​​,
(73)
where the square root on the right is the principal square root. Its argument never lies on the nonpositive real axis for z∈D, so this defines the required holomorphic function. Then g(z)=(z+s(z))/2∼z.
The two quadratic roots have product a2. For z∈/S, neither root lies on ∣ζ∣=a, since that circle maps into S. Consequently exactly one root lies outside the circle, and it is the branch g chosen at infinity. Also, if two exterior points have the same image, then
(ζ1​−ζ2​)(1−ζ1​ζ2​a2​)=0,
(74)
whose second factor cannot vanish. Thus the Joukowski map is a conformal map from ∣ζ∣>a onto D, and g is conformal throughout D. The two endpoints are branch points and are excluded.
The complex potential in the circle plane is the sum of the uniform flow term Ue−iαζ, its circle-image term Ua2eiα/ζ, and the point vortex term −iΓlogζ/(2π). On ζ=aeiθ, the first two sum to 2Uacos(θ−α), which is real, while the imaginary part of the vortex term is the constant −Γloga/(2π). Hence the circle is a streamline, giving no normal flow. At infinity the first term gives the required uniform flow; the logarithmic term supplies circulation Γ. The potential may be multivalued by a real constant, but its velocity is single-valued.
Conformal transport therefore gives
w(z)=U(g(z)e−iα+g(z)a2eiα​)−2πiΓ​logg(z).​
(75)
In the frame where the plate is horizontal, its length is 4a and the stream has angle α; rotating the frame gives the equivalent incidence description. The complex velocity is
dzdw​=1−a2/ζ2W′(ζ)​.
(76)
At the trailing edge z=2a, corresponding to ζ=a, the denominator has a simple zero. Finite velocity requires
0=W′(a)=−2iUsinα−2πaiΓ​,
(77)
so the Kutta condition is
Γ=−4πUasinα.​
(78)
With this choice, cancellation of the common zero gives
dzdw​​z=2a​=2/aW′′(a)​=Ueiα+4πaiΓ​=Ucosα​.
(79)
Thus the limiting velocity has zero transverse component and is tangent to the plate.

i OurBigBook.com
Given Xn​=k>0, the number remaining next time is uniform on {0,…,k−1} and is independent of earlier choices; given Xn​=0, the next state is 0. Thus the conditional law of Xn+1​ depends only on Xn​, which is the Markov property.
By contrast, observing only the last number removed generally loses information about the remaining stock. For N≥3, compare the two positive-probability histories
(Y1​,Y2​)=(1,1),(Y1​,Y2​)=(N−1,1).
(104)
Both have Y2​=1, but the first leaves N−2>0 stickers, so P(Y3​>0∣Y1​=1,Y2​=1)=1, whereas the second leaves none, so P(Y3​>0∣Y1​=N−1,Y2​=1)=0. Hence (Yn​) fails the Markov property.
The qualification N≥3 is necessary if a Markov chain is allowed to have time-dependent transitions. For N=1, the removal sequence is the deterministic, time-homogeneous Markov chain 1,0,0,…. For N=2, it is a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain, although it is not time-homogeneous on its observed removal states: a removal of 1 at the first step forces another removal of 1, whereas a removal of 1 at the second step forces 0 next. The blanket non-Markov claim should therefore be understood in the generic, nondegenerate setting.

The Gaussian linear model has log likelihood function, up to an additive constant,
ℓ(θ,σ2)=−2n​logσ2−2σ21​(Y−Xθ)T(Y−Xθ).
(120)
For each fixed positive σ2, maximize this by minimizing the residual sum of squares. Differentiation gives the normal equations
XTXθ=XTY.
(121)
The full column rank of X makes XTX positive definite, hence invertible, so
θ=(XTX)−1XTY.​
(122)
The quadratic objective is strictly convex, which proves uniqueness. The joint maximum-likelihood estimate has the same coefficient estimate, except on the probability-zero event of an exactly zero residual when the positive-variance likelihood has no finite joint maximizer.

θ=θ+Aϵ.

Thus θ is an unbiased estimator. In addition, the multivariate normal distribution is preserved by linear maps, so θ is multivariate normal with the displayed mean and covariance matrix.

To justify its denominator, let H=X(XTX)−1XT, the orthogonal projection matrix onto the column space of X. Then the residual is (I−H)ϵ. The idempotent matrix I−H has rank n−p, so diagonalizing it with an orthogonal matrix gives
σ2∥Y−Xθ∥2​∼χn−p2​.

Consequently Es2=σ2, making s2 an unbiased estimator. If specifically asked for maximum likelihood estimation, maximizing over σ2 gives the alternative σML2​=∥Y−Xθ∥2/n, which is biased downward by the factor (n−p)/n.

Zi​=σvi​​θi​−θi​​∼N(0,1).

a OurBigBook.com
A polynomial least-squares approximation pn​∈Πn​ minimizes the weighted residual norm:
∥u−pn​∥=q∈Πn​min​∥u−q∥.​
(130)
Equivalently it minimizes ∫−11​x2(u(x)−q(x))2dx. This is a best approximation within a finite-dimensional polynomial space, without an interpolation requirement.

b

Words: 130 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 130
b OurBigBook.com
If p is a minimizer, then for each q∈Πn​ the quadratic
∥u−p−tq∥2=∥u−p∥2−2t(u−p,q)+t2∥q∥2
(131)
has a minimum at t=0, so (u−p,q)=0. Conversely, if this orthogonality holds, then for every q∈Πn​ the Pythagorean theorem in the inner product space gives
∥u−q∥2=∥u−p∥2+∥p−q∥2≥∥u−p∥2.
(132)
Thus the minimizers are exactly the orthogonal projections characterized by
(u−p,q)=0for all q∈Πn​.​
(133)
For existence, write p=∑j=0n​cj​xj. The conditions form the normal equations Gc=b, with Gram matrix Gij​=(xi,xj) and bi​=(u,xi). For every nonzero coefficient vector v,
vTGv=∫−11​x2(∑j​vj​xj)2dx>0.
(134)
Indeed a nonzero polynomial is nonzero on some open interval away from 0, where the weight is positive. Hence G is a positive-definite matrix and is invertible, proving existence and uniqueness of c. Uniqueness also follows from the preceding Pythagorean theorem identity. The zero of the weight at one point therefore causes no degeneracy on continuous functions or polynomials.

p(−x)=−p(x).​

For w=0, the Householder transformation is
H(w)=I−2wTwwwT​.​

Let P=wwT/(wTw). Then PT=P and P2=P, since P is the orthogonal projection matrix onto the span of w. Hence HT=H and

Thus H is a symmetric matrix and an orthogonal matrix. Geometrically it reverses the component parallel to w and fixes the perpendicular hyperplane.

Apply part (b) to the first column of A, using the identity if it is already the zero vector. This gives an orthogonal matrix H1​ for which H1​A has zeros below its first diagonal entry. At stage j, apply a Householder transformation to rows j,…,n of column j, and extend it by the identity on the first j−1 coordinates. If that trailing column is zero, again use the identity. The transformation preserves zeros in earlier columns, since their trailing entries already vanish.
After at most n−1 stages,
R=Hn−1​⋯H1​A
(144)
is an upper triangular matrix. Each Hj​ is symmetric and orthogonal, so with
Q=H1​⋯Hn−1​
(145)
we have QTQ=I and
A=QR.​
(146)
No invertibility assumption was used, so the Householder QR decomposition also exists for singular matrices.

d

Solution
Words: 109
d OurBigBook.com
Multiply Ax=b by QT to get the equivalent triangular system
Rx=QTb.
(147)
For nonsingular A, compute c=QTb and use back substitution:
xi​=Rii​ci​−∑j=i+1n​Rij​xj​​,i=n,n−1,…,1.
(148)
Orthogonal transformations preserve the Euclidean norm, making this a numerically stable reduction. The factors can be applied as stored Householder transformations without explicitly forming Q.
Since Q is invertible, A is singular exactly when R is singular. For an upper triangular matrix,
detR=∏i=1n​Rii​.
(149)
Thus a singular A forces at least one zero diagonal entry in R. In that case, ordinary division-based back substitution must be replaced by a consistency/rank analysis: the system may have no solution or infinitely many solutions, and a rank-revealing factorization can identify the free parameters.
